stem: A 3.8 kg baby is delivered at a THQ hospital after a difficult delivery with shoulder dystocia. On examination the right arm hangs by the side, adducted and internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. The grasp reflex is present. Which part of the brachial plexus is most likely injured?
explanation: The 'waiter's tip' posture of Erb's palsy results from traction on the upper trunk: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps and brachialis lose C5–C6 supply, so the arm is adducted, medially rotated and the elbow extended. A lower trunk injury spares these shoulder and elbow muscles and instead paralyses the small muscles of the hand, so the grasp would be lost.

stem: Bilal, 24, fell from a tree and grabbed a branch with his left hand to break the fall, forcefully abducting the arm. He now has wasting and weakness of the small muscles of the left hand, numbness along the medial forearm, and a drooping left eyelid with a small left pupil. Which spinal roots are most likely injured?
explanation: Forceful upward traction on the arm injures the lower trunk (Klumpke's palsy): C8 and T1 supply the intrinsic hand muscles and the medial forearm skin. Ptosis and miosis indicate Horner's syndrome from T1 root avulsion close to the sympathetic chain. A C5–C6 injury would affect shoulder abduction and elbow flexion instead.

stem: A 68-year-old woman in Lahore falls on her outstretched hand and sustains a fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus. A week later she cannot abduct the arm beyond the first few degrees, and she has reduced sensation over the lower lateral aspect of the shoulder. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus with the posterior circumflex humeral artery, so it is at risk in this fracture. It supplies deltoid and the skin over its lower half (the 'regimental badge' area). The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus but has no cutaneous area on the shoulder and is not related to the surgical neck.

stem: A 30-year-old motorcyclist has a closed fracture of the middle third of the right humeral shaft. He cannot extend his wrist or the metacarpophalangeal joints and has numbness over the dorsum of the first web space. Which muscle is most likely to retain normal power?
explanation: In the spiral groove the radial nerve has already given its branches to triceps in the axilla and upper arm, so elbow extension is usually preserved while wrist drop results. Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus are supplied just above the lateral epicondyle, below the spiral groove, so they are weak as well.

stem: A 7-year-old boy has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. After reduction he can flex his wrist and has normal sensation in the hand, but he cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb or the distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger, so he cannot make a round 'O' with thumb and index finger. Which nerve is most likely injured?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
explanation: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve supplies flexor pollicis longus, the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus, and it has no cutaneous branch, so the deficit is purely motor. It is the nerve most often injured in supracondylar fractures. A posterior interosseous lesion would cause finger and thumb extension weakness instead.

stem: A 45-year-old carpenter has an old fracture of the medial epicondyle of the humerus. When asked to grip a sheet of paper between his thumb and the side of his index finger, he flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb to hold it. Weakness of which muscle explains this sign?
explanation: Froment's sign shows weakness of adductor pollicis, supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve; the patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus (median nerve), which flexes the thumb's interphalangeal joint. Flexor pollicis longus is therefore working, not weak, and the other two thenar muscles are median-supplied.

stem: Rukhsana, 32 weeks pregnant, has tingling of her right thumb, index and middle fingers that wakes her at night. Tapping over the front of the wrist reproduces the tingling. Sensation over the skin of the thenar eminence is normal. Which anatomical fact best explains the normal sensation over the thenar eminence?
options: The recurrent motor branch carries no sensory fibres
The skin of the thenar eminence is supplied by the radial nerve only
The palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
The digital nerves arise proximal to the carpal tunnel
explanation: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises in the forearm and runs superficial to the flexor retinaculum, so it escapes compression in carpal tunnel syndrome and keeps the central and lateral palm sensate. The digital nerves arise distal to the tunnel, which is why the fingers are affected. The recurrent branch is motor, but that does not explain preserved skin sensation.

stem: A 52-year-old woman has had a mastectomy with axillary node clearance for breast cancer. At follow-up, the medial border of her scapula lifts away from the chest wall when she pushes against a wall with outstretched arms. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) runs on the superficial surface of serratus anterior on the medial wall of the axilla, where it can be injured during axillary clearance. Paralysis of serratus anterior lets the medial border of the scapula wing. The thoracodorsal nerve is also at risk in the axilla, but it supplies latissimus dorsi and does not cause winging.

stem: A 26-year-old man has a stab wound in the upper lateral arm. He has weak elbow flexion and weak supination with the elbow flexed, and reduced sensation over the lateral side of the forearm. The biceps jerk is diminished. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies biceps, brachialis and coracobrachialis and ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, which fits all the findings. Brachioradialis (radial nerve) still allows some elbow flexion. A radial nerve lesion would cause wrist drop and loss of sensation on the dorsum of the hand rather than the lateral forearm.

stem: A 63-year-old man has right shoulder pain after lifting a heavy box. He cannot start abduction of the right arm from the side, but once the examiner passively lifts the arm to about 30°, he can continue abducting it himself. Which tendon is most likely torn?
explanation: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15° or so of abduction; beyond that deltoid takes over, so a patient with a supraspinatus tear can continue abduction once the arm is started passively. Infraspinatus is a lateral rotator and subscapularis a medial rotator, so their tears affect rotation rather than the start of abduction.

stem: A 22-year-old cricketer has his anterior shoulder dislocation reduced in the emergency department. Before and after reduction, the doctor should specifically test sensation over which area to check the nerve most at risk?
options: Skin over the lower part of the deltoid
Dorsum of the first web space
explanation: In anterior dislocation the humeral head is displaced forwards and downwards, stretching the axillary nerve where it runs just below the joint capsule. Its cutaneous branch (upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm) supplies the skin over the lower deltoid, which is quick to test. The first web space tests the radial nerve, which is less commonly injured in shoulder dislocation.

stem: A 19-year-old student falls on her outstretched hand. She has tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox, but initial wrist radiographs are normal. A repeat image two weeks later shows a fracture through the waist of the scaphoid. Which complication is she most at risk of because of the bone's blood supply?
options: Avascular necrosis of the proximal fragment
Avascular necrosis of the distal fragment
explanation: Most of the scaphoid's blood supply enters at its distal end and flows retrogradely, so a waist fracture can deprive the proximal pole, leading to avascular necrosis and non-union. The distal fragment keeps its supply. Extensor pollicis longus rupture is a recognised late complication of distal radius fractures, not scaphoid fractures.

stem: A 66-year-old woman had a minimally displaced fracture of the distal radius treated in a cast. Eight weeks later she suddenly cannot extend the interphalangeal joint of her thumb while the other fingers extend normally. Which structure has most likely failed?
explanation: Extensor pollicis longus turns around the dorsal (Lister's) tubercle of the radius, a zone with poor blood supply; after a distal radius fracture the tendon may fray and rupture weeks later. It is the only tendon that extends the thumb's interphalangeal joint. Extensor pollicis brevis acts on the metacarpophalangeal joint, and a posterior interosseous lesion would weaken finger extension too.

stem: A 35-year-old cyclist who rides long distances has weakness of finger abduction and adduction and wasting of the first dorsal interosseous. Sensation over the dorsal and medial side of the hand is normal, and flexor digitorum profundus to the little finger is strong. Where is the ulnar nerve most likely compressed?
options: Between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
explanation: The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve arises about 5 cm above the wrist, and the branch to flexor digitorum profundus arises in the forearm, so both are spared when the nerve is compressed in Guyon's canal, as from pressure on handlebars. A lesion at the elbow or between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris would weaken FDP to the little finger and reduce dorsal hand sensation. The ulnar nerve does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

stem: A 9-year-old girl had a supracondylar fracture managed in an above-elbow cast. Six months later her fingers and wrist are held flexed, and the fingers can be extended only when the wrist is flexed further. Which muscles are mainly affected by this complication?
options: Wrist and finger extensors of the forearm
explanation: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture follows compartment ischaemia after brachial artery compromise; the deep flexor compartment (flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus) is most affected and is replaced by fibrous tissue. The shortened flexors explain why the fingers extend only when the wrist is flexed. The extensor compartment is less often involved.

stem: A nurse at a BHU is drawing blood from the median cubital vein. Which structure lies between this vein and the brachial artery and protects the artery during venepuncture?
explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis passes from the biceps tendon medially across the cubital fossa, separating the superficial median cubital vein from the deeper brachial artery and median nerve. Pronator teres forms the medial boundary of the fossa and does not lie between vein and artery.

stem: A 50-year-old man needs femoral venous access during resuscitation. The femoral artery pulse is palpable just below the inguinal ligament. Where should the needle be inserted relative to the pulse?
options: Above the inguinal ligament over the pulse
explanation: Within the femoral sheath the order from lateral to medial is artery, vein and femoral canal, with the femoral nerve outside the sheath laterally. The vein therefore lies medial to the palpable artery just below the inguinal ligament. Puncturing above the ligament risks retroperitoneal bleeding.

stem: A house officer wants to palpate the femoral artery pulse in a shocked patient. At which surface landmark is the pulse best felt?
options: Just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine
explanation: The femoral artery enters the thigh behind the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, halfway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The midpoint of the inguinal ligament (between the ASIS and pubic tubercle) is a slightly more lateral landmark that marks the deep inguinal ring.

stem: A 28-year-old man with a fractured tibia is managed in a tight above-knee plaster cast. Two days later he cannot dorsiflex his ankle or extend his toes, and the foot is slightly inverted. Sensation is reduced over the dorsum of the foot. Where has the nerve most likely been compressed?
options: In the popliteal fossa at the knee crease
Around the neck of the fibula
explanation: The common fibular (peroneal) nerve winds superficially around the neck of the fibula, where a tight cast or a fracture can compress it, causing foot drop, loss of eversion and sensory loss over the dorsum of the foot. Compression behind the medial malleolus affects the tibial nerve and the sole of the foot instead.

stem: After an intramuscular injection given into the buttock, a 40-year-old man notices that when he stands on his right leg alone, the left side of his pelvis drops. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
explanation: Gluteus medius and minimus of the stance leg keep the pelvis level; when they are paralysed, the pelvis drops on the opposite, unsupported side (positive Trendelenburg sign). A drop on the left when standing on the right therefore points to the right superior gluteal nerve. The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which does not stabilise the pelvis in this way.

stem: A nurse is teaching students at a nursing school where to give an intramuscular injection into the gluteal region. Which site is safest to avoid injuring the sciatic nerve?
options: Lower medial quadrant of the buttock
Upper outer quadrant of the buttock
Lower lateral quadrant of the buttock
Upper inner quadrant of the buttock
explanation: The sciatic nerve emerges below piriformis and runs down through the lower medial part of the buttock, so the upper outer quadrant is the traditional safe site. Injections in the lower or medial parts risk sciatic nerve injury and foot drop.

stem: A 55-year-old woman undergoes pelvic lymph node dissection for cervical cancer. Afterwards she has difficulty bringing her right thigh towards the midline and a patch of numbness on the medial side of the right thigh. Which nerve has been injured?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation: The obturator nerve runs along the lateral pelvic wall to the obturator foramen, close to pelvic lymph nodes; it supplies the adductor muscles and an area of skin on the medial thigh. The femoral nerve would cause weak knee extension and numbness of the anterior thigh.

stem: A 60-year-old man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation develops a right psoas haematoma. He has difficulty climbing stairs because his knee buckles, the right knee jerk is absent, and he has numbness over the front of the thigh and the medial side of the leg. Which nerve is compressed?
explanation: The femoral nerve (L2–L4) runs in the groove between psoas and iliacus, where a haematoma can compress it. It supplies quadriceps (knee extension and the knee jerk), the anterior thigh skin and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial leg. The obturator nerve also arises from L2–L4 but supplies the adductors and medial thigh.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has burning pain and numbness of the sole of her left foot that is worse on standing. Tapping behind and below the medial malleolus reproduces the symptoms. Which nerve is compressed?
explanation: The tibial nerve passes behind the medial malleolus beneath the flexor retinaculum (tarsal tunnel) and divides into the medial and lateral plantar nerves supplying the sole. The saphenous nerve also runs near the medial malleolus but in front of it, and supplies the medial side of the leg and foot, not the sole.

stem: A 23-year-old footballer injures his knee when another player falls against its lateral side. The examiner finds that the tibia can be drawn forward on the femur with the knee flexed to 90°. Which ligament is torn?
explanation: The anterior cruciate ligament prevents anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur, so a positive anterior drawer test indicates its rupture. A blow to the lateral knee often also tears the medial collateral ligament and medial meniscus, but the medial collateral ligament is tested by valgus stress, not the drawer test.

stem: A 34-year-old man stands up from a squatting position while twisting on his flexed right knee. He now has medial joint line pain and the knee intermittently locks. Why is the medial meniscus injured more often than the lateral meniscus?
options: It is attached to the tibial collateral ligament and is less mobile
It is thinner and has no blood supply at all
It is attached to the tendon of popliteus
It is not attached to the tibia at its horns
explanation: The medial meniscus is firmly attached to the deep part of the tibial (medial) collateral ligament and the joint capsule, so it cannot move away from rotational forces and is trapped between femur and tibia. The lateral meniscus is the more mobile one because popliteus pulls it backwards during flexion. Both menisci have a vascular outer rim.

stem: At the start of flexion from full extension, the locked knee must first be 'unlocked' by lateral rotation of the femur on the fixed tibia. Which muscle performs this action?
explanation: Popliteus laterally rotates the femur on the tibia (or medially rotates the tibia when the foot is free), unlocking the knee from its screw-home position so flexion can begin. Biceps femoris flexes the knee and laterally rotates the tibia, so it does not unlock the extended joint.

stem: A 72-year-old woman has a displaced intracapsular fracture of the neck of the femur after a fall at home. The surgeon chooses a hip replacement rather than fixation because of the high risk of avascular necrosis of the femoral head. Which artery normally provides most of the blood supply to the adult femoral head?
options: Artery of the ligamentum teres from the obturator artery
explanation: Retinacular branches, mainly from the medial circumflex femoral artery, run along the femoral neck under the capsule to supply the head; a displaced intracapsular fracture tears them. The artery of the ligamentum teres contributes little in adults and cannot sustain the head on its own.

stem: Imran, 30, is a front-seat passenger in a road traffic accident in which his knee strikes the dashboard. His right leg is shortened, flexed, adducted and medially rotated at the hip, and he cannot dorsiflex the right foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
explanation: A force along the femur with the hip flexed drives the femoral head backwards (posterior dislocation), producing the shortened, flexed, adducted and medially rotated limb. The sciatic nerve lies directly behind the hip joint and is stretched, often its common fibular part, causing foot drop. Femoral nerve injury is more typical of anterior dislocation.

stem: A surgeon performs a venous cut-down on the great saphenous vein just in front of the medial malleolus in a child with collapsed peripheral veins. Afterwards the child's mother notices that the skin along the medial border of the foot is numb. Which nerve was injured?
explanation: The saphenous nerve, the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, accompanies the great saphenous vein in front of the medial malleolus and supplies the skin of the medial leg and medial border of the foot. The sural nerve accompanies the small saphenous vein behind the lateral malleolus.

stem: A 45-year-old teacher with varicose veins is scheduled for ligation at the saphenofemoral junction. Through which opening does the great saphenous vein pass to join the femoral vein?
options: Saphenous opening in the fascia lata
explanation: The great saphenous vein passes through the saphenous opening, a gap in the fascia lata about 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, and drains into the femoral vein. The femoral ring is the upper opening of the femoral canal, and the adductor hiatus transmits the femoral vessels to the popliteal fossa.

stem: A 25-year-old man has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the femur. The foot is cold and pale, and the pedal pulses are absent. Which structure in the popliteal fossa is most at risk because it lies deepest, directly against the bone?
explanation: From superficial to deep, the popliteal fossa contains the tibial nerve, the popliteal vein and then the popliteal artery, which lies on the popliteal surface of the femur and the capsule of the knee. It is therefore easily injured by supracondylar fractures and knee dislocations, as the cold, pulseless foot shows.

stem: A 38-year-old labourer has low back pain radiating down the back of the right leg to the dorsum of the foot. He has weakness of extension of the great toe and reduced sensation over the dorsum of the foot and first web space. The ankle and knee jerks are normal. Which nerve root is most likely compressed?
explanation: Weak great toe extension (extensor hallucis longus) and numbness of the dorsum of the foot are typical of an L5 root lesion, usually from a posterolateral L4/L5 disc prolapse compressing the traversing L5 root. An S1 lesion would reduce the ankle jerk and cause numbness of the lateral border and sole of the foot.

stem: A 41-year-old woman has sciatica with numbness of the lateral border of the right foot, weakness of plantarflexion and an absent right ankle jerk. MRI shows a posterolateral disc prolapse. At which level is the prolapse most likely?
explanation: These are S1 root signs. A posterolateral prolapse usually compresses the root that exits one level below, so the S1 root is compressed by an L5/S1 disc. An L4/L5 prolapse typically compresses L5, producing weak great toe extension with a preserved ankle jerk.

stem: A lumbar puncture is performed on a 30-year-old woman with suspected meningitis, with the needle inserted in the midline between the L3 and L4 spinous processes. Which layer is the last one pierced before cerebrospinal fluid flows?
explanation: The midline needle passes through skin, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural space, dura mater and then arachnoid mater to enter the subarachnoid space, which contains CSF. Dura and arachnoid are closely applied, but the arachnoid is the last layer crossed. The pia mater lines the cord and roots and is not pierced.

stem: A 17-year-old girl twists her right ankle when her foot rolls inwards on an uneven road. She has swelling and tenderness just in front of and below the lateral malleolus. Which ligament is most likely injured?
explanation: Inversion with plantarflexion stresses the lateral ligament complex, and the anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest and the first to tear, giving tenderness in front of the lateral malleolus. The deltoid ligament is on the medial side and is injured by eversion.

stem: A surgeon must ligate the axillary artery to control bleeding from a stab wound in the axilla. Ligation at which site is most likely to preserve the blood supply of the upper limb through the scapular anastomosis?
options: Distal to the origin of the subscapular artery
Proximal to the origin of the subscapular artery
Distal to the origin of the profunda brachii artery
Distal to the origin of the anterior circumflex humeral artery
explanation: The anastomosis around the scapula links branches of the subclavian artery (suprascapular and dorsal scapular arteries) with the subscapular artery from the third part of the axillary artery. If the ligature is proximal to the subscapular artery, blood can reach the distal axillary artery through this anastomosis. Ligation distal to the subscapular origin bypasses the anastomosis and risks ischaemia.

stem: A 33-year-old man has a closed fracture of the tibial shaft. Six hours after admission he has severe pain on passive plantarflexion of the toes and numbness between the first and second toes. Which compartment of the leg is affected?
explanation: Passive plantarflexion stretches the anterior compartment muscles (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus), and the deep fibular nerve in this compartment supplies the first web space. The deep posterior compartment would be stretched by passive dorsiflexion of the toes and would affect the sole.

stem: A 28-year-old woman falls on her outstretched hand. Radiographs show the lunate displaced anteriorly into the carpal tunnel. Which nerve is she at greatest risk of having compressed?
explanation: The lunate lies directly behind the carpal tunnel, so anterior dislocation pushes it into the tunnel, causing acute median nerve compression with tingling of the lateral three and a half fingers. The ulnar nerve passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum in Guyon's canal and is less affected.

stem: A 52-year-old man is having a supraclavicular brachial plexus block. Shortly afterwards he becomes breathless and the right hemidiaphragm is found to be paralysed. Spread of local anaesthetic to which nerve explains this?
explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) descends on the anterior surface of scalenus anterior close to the brachial plexus roots and trunks, so local anaesthetic often spreads to it in interscalene and supraclavicular blocks, causing ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis. The long thoracic and dorsal scapular nerves supply serratus anterior and the rhomboids, not the diaphragm.

stem: A 35-year-old rock climber has difficulty pulling his body up and cannot press his arm against his side forcefully after an axillary injury. Extension, adduction and medial rotation of the shoulder are weak. Which nerve is damaged?
explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C6–C8, from the posterior cord) supplies latissimus dorsi, the main extensor, adductor and medial rotator of the arm used in climbing. The axillary nerve supplies deltoid and teres minor, whose loss mainly weakens abduction.

stem: A 9-year-old boy falls on his outstretched hand and sustains a fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head. He cannot extend his fingers at the metacarpophalangeal joints, but he can extend his wrist, and sensation in the hand is normal. Which nerve is injured?
options: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
explanation: The posterior interosseous (deep radial) nerve winds around the neck of the radius through supinator and is at risk with radial head dislocation. It supplies finger and thumb extensors but has no cutaneous branch; extensor carpi radialis longus is supplied above the elbow, so wrist extension is preserved. A main radial nerve lesion would cause wrist drop and sensory loss.

stem: A medical student is learning surface anatomy of the wrist. The pulse of which artery can be felt in the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
explanation: The radial artery passes from the front of the wrist to the dorsum through the anatomical snuffbox, lying on the scaphoid and trapezium, before entering the palm between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous. The ulnar artery stays on the medial, palmar side of the wrist.

stem: A 40-year-old volleyball player has an MRI showing a ganglion cyst in the suprascapular notch. He has weak abduction in the first few degrees and weak lateral rotation of the arm, with wasting above and below the spine of the scapula. Which nerve is injured?
explanation: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus (initiation of abduction) and infraspinatus (lateral rotation), so wasting above and below the scapular spine is typical. The axillary nerve supplies teres minor and deltoid, so its loss would cause deltoid wasting and weak abduction beyond 15° instead.

stem: From which structures is the brachial plexus formed?
options: Dorsal rami of C5 to T1
Ventral rami of C4 to C8
Ventral rami of C5 to T1
Dorsal rami of C4 to C8
explanation: The brachial plexus is formed by the ventral (anterior) rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1, which form trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches. Dorsal rami supply the deep back muscles and skin of the back and do not contribute.

stem: A 50-year-old man with a lesion of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus is examined. Which pair of muscles would you expect to be weak?
options: Deltoid and extensor carpi radialis longus
Flexor carpi ulnaris and adductor pollicis
explanation: The posterior cord gives the axillary nerve (deltoid, teres minor) and the radial nerve (extensors of the elbow, wrist and fingers, including extensor carpi radialis longus), as well as the subscapular and thoracodorsal nerves. Biceps and coracobrachialis are supplied by the lateral cord via the musculocutaneous nerve.

stem: A 27-year-old man cuts the front of his wrist on broken glass. He cannot bring the pulp of his thumb against the pulp of his little finger, and the thenar eminence is flattened. Which nerve has been divided?
explanation: At the wrist the median nerve gives the recurrent branch to the thenar muscles (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis), so division causes loss of opposition and an 'ape thumb'. The anterior interosseous nerve arises in the forearm and does not supply the thenar muscles.

stem: Two patients have ulnar nerve injuries: one at the elbow and one at the wrist. The patient with the wrist injury has more marked clawing of the ring and little fingers. What is the best explanation?
options: The lumbricals to the ring and little fingers are spared in wrist lesions
The interossei are spared in elbow lesions
Flexor digitorum superficialis is paralysed only in elbow lesions
The medial half of flexor digitorum profundus still works in wrist lesions
explanation: Clawing results from unopposed long flexors and extensors when the interossei and medial lumbricals are paralysed. In a wrist lesion the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus (supplied in the forearm) still flexes the distal interphalangeal joints, so the claw is worse; in an elbow lesion FDP is also weak, the 'ulnar paradox'. Flexor digitorum superficialis is supplied by the median nerve.

stem: A 60-year-old man has a flexion deformity of the ring finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint with a palpable cord in the palm. Thickening and contracture of which structure causes this condition?
explanation: Dupuytren's contracture is a fibroproliferative thickening of the palmar aponeurosis and its digital extensions, most often affecting the ring and little fingers. The tendons and their sheaths are not primarily involved, so the deformity is not due to flexor tendon disease.

stem: A 35-year-old farmer has a pin-prick injury of the little finger that leads to infection of the flexor tendon sheath. The swelling later spreads to the palm and the front of the lower forearm. Into which space has the infection spread?
explanation: The synovial sheath of the little finger is usually continuous with the ulnar bursa, which surrounds the long flexor tendons in the palm and extends proximally behind the flexor retinaculum into the forearm. The thumb's sheath continues into the radial bursa instead.

stem: An orthopaedic surgeon asks a patient to place the back of his hand on his lower back and then lift the hand away from the back. The patient cannot lift it away. Which rotator cuff muscle is being tested?
explanation: The lift-off test assesses subscapularis, the main medial rotator of the shoulder, by asking the patient to medially rotate further from the hand-behind-back position. Infraspinatus and teres minor are lateral rotators and are tested by resisted lateral rotation.

stem: An 11-year-old boy falls on his shoulder and fractures his clavicle at the junction of its middle and lateral thirds. The medial fragment is displaced upwards. Which muscle pulls the medial fragment upwards?
explanation: Sternocleidomastoid attaches to the medial third of the clavicle and elevates the medial fragment. The lateral fragment is pulled down by the weight of the limb and drawn medially by pectoralis major. Subclavius lies under the clavicle and helps protect the subclavian vessels rather than elevating the fragment.

stem: When measuring blood pressure with a stethoscope, where is the brachial artery best heard at the elbow?
options: Medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
Lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
explanation: In the cubital fossa the brachial artery lies immediately medial to the biceps tendon, with the median nerve medial to the artery. The ulnar nerve, not an artery, lies behind the medial epicondyle.

stem: A 3-year-old girl cries and refuses to use her left arm after her father swung her up by the hands. The arm is held slightly flexed and pronated. The radial head has slipped partly out of which ligament?
explanation: In 'pulled elbow' a sudden pull on the extended arm makes the small radial head slip partly through the annular ligament, which encircles it and holds it against the ulna. It is reduced by supination with flexion. The radial collateral ligament blends with the annular ligament but does not encircle the head.

stem: A 65-year-old man has used a badly fitted crutch that pressed into his axilla for several weeks. He has wrist drop. Which additional finding would best indicate that the lesion is in the axilla rather than in the spiral groove?
options: Loss of sensation on the dorsum of the first web space
explanation: Branches to triceps leave the radial nerve in the axilla and upper arm, so they are paralysed by a high (axillary) lesion but usually spared in a spiral groove lesion. Loss of web space sensation, weak finger extension and weak brachioradialis occur with lesions at both levels.

stem: Which structure lies lateral to the femoral sheath and is therefore not enclosed by it?
explanation: The femoral sheath, a downward extension of transversalis and iliac fascia, encloses the femoral artery, femoral vein and femoral canal (with its lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath in the femoral triangle, which matters for femoral nerve blocks.

stem: An anaesthetist performs an adductor canal block for knee surgery. Which nerve, running with the femoral artery in the canal, is the main target of this block?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation: The adductor (subsartorial) canal contains the femoral artery and vein, the saphenous nerve and the nerve to vastus medialis. The block anaesthetises the saphenous nerve while largely sparing quadriceps power. The obturator nerve lies medial to the canal among the adductors.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a low chair, but walks on level ground without a limp. Hip extension against resistance is weak. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, the powerful hip extensor used to rise from sitting and climb stairs, while ordinary walking relies little on it. The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius and minimus, and its injury produces a Trendelenburg gait.

stem: A 33-year-old man has a complete sciatic nerve injury at the greater sciatic notch from a gunshot wound. Which movement is most likely to be preserved?
explanation: Knee extension is performed by quadriceps, supplied by the femoral nerve, so it is preserved. The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings (knee flexion) and, through its tibial and common fibular divisions, all muscles below the knee. Some weak knee flexion may remain through gracilis and sartorius, but it is markedly reduced.

stem: A 21-year-old woman twists her ankle with the foot forced outwards. She has tenderness over the medial malleolus, and an X-ray shows a small avulsed fragment from its tip. Which ligament is attached at this site?
explanation: The deltoid (medial collateral) ligament is attached to the medial malleolus and is very strong, so forced eversion often avulses the tip of the malleolus rather than tearing the ligament. The talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments are lateral and are injured by inversion.

stem: A 29-year-old man's flexed knee strikes the dashboard in a car crash. The tibia sags backwards on the femur when the knee is flexed to 90°. Which ligament is torn?
explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament prevents backward displacement of the tibia on the femur; a blow to the front of the flexed knee drives the tibia backwards and tears it, giving a posterior sag and positive posterior drawer test. The anterior cruciate ligament resists forward displacement.

stem: A medical officer checks peripheral pulses in a diabetic patient in Multan. Where is the dorsalis pedis pulse usually felt?
options: Just lateral to the tendon of extensor hallucis longus
Just medial to the tendon of tibialis anterior on the leg
explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery, the continuation of the anterior tibial artery, is palpable on the dorsum of the foot just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon, over the tarsal bones. The posterior tibial pulse is felt behind the medial malleolus.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is advised to perform calf exercises while bedbound after surgery to reduce the risk of deep vein thrombosis. Which muscle, containing large venous sinuses, is most important in the calf muscle pump?
explanation: Soleus contains large venous sinuses and, enclosed in deep fascia, compresses the deep veins with each contraction, driving blood towards the heart; it is often called the 'peripheral heart'. Stasis in these soleal sinuses is a common starting point for DVT. Tibialis anterior lies in the anterior compartment and contributes little to venous return.

stem: A 16-year-old fast bowler has low back pain. Imaging shows a forward slip of the L5 vertebral body over S1 with a defect between the superior and inferior articular processes of L5. Which part of the vertebra is defective?
explanation: Spondylolysis is a stress fracture of the pars interarticularis, the part of the lamina between the superior and inferior articular processes; bilateral defects allow the body to slip forwards (spondylolisthesis), most often at L5/S1. The pedicle connects the body to the arch and is not the usual site.

stem: During a lumbar epidural for labour analgesia, the anaesthetist feels a sudden loss of resistance to injection as the needle enters the epidural space. Which ligament has the needle just passed through?
explanation: The dense, elastic ligamentum flavum joins adjacent laminae and forms the posterior boundary of the epidural space; passing through it gives the characteristic loss of resistance. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies on the front of the canal behind the vertebral bodies and is not crossed by a midline epidural needle.

stem: A 48-year-old man has neck pain radiating to the middle finger. Triceps power is reduced and the triceps jerk is diminished. The biceps jerk is normal. Which nerve root is compressed?
explanation: C7 supplies triceps and the triceps jerk, and its dermatome includes the middle finger; it is usually compressed by a C6/C7 disc. A C6 lesion reduces the biceps and supinator jerks and causes numbness of the thumb and index finger.

stem: Which ligament is the strongest ligament of the hip joint and prevents hyperextension when standing?
explanation: The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament, running from the anterior inferior iliac spine to the intertrochanteric line, is the strongest ligament in the body and tightens in extension, allowing upright posture with little muscular effort. The ligamentum teres is weak and mainly carries a small artery.

stem: A 37-year-old woman develops numbness and pain over the anterolateral thigh after gaining weight and wearing a tight belt. Power and reflexes are normal. Which nerve is most likely compressed as it passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine?
options: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
explanation: Meralgia paraesthetica is compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2–L3) where it passes under or through the inguinal ligament just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. It is purely sensory, which explains normal power and reflexes. A femoral nerve lesion would weaken quadriceps and reduce the knee jerk.

stem: A 26-year-old man has a laceration of the lateral leg just below the fibular head that divides the superficial fibular nerve only. Which deficit would you expect?
options: Weak eversion and numbness over most of the dorsum of the foot
Foot drop with numbness of the first web space
Weak plantarflexion and numbness of the sole
Weak inversion and numbness of the heel
explanation: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis (eversion) and the skin over most of the dorsum of the foot except the first web space. Foot drop with first web space numbness indicates the deep fibular nerve, which supplies the anterior compartment.

stem: A 59-year-old man needs a coronary artery bypass graft, and the surgeon plans to use his great saphenous vein. The patient asks whether removing it will affect venous drainage of his leg. Which fact makes harvesting this vein generally safe?
options: The great saphenous vein carries most of the leg's venous return
The perforating veins direct flow from deep to superficial veins
The deep veins carry most of the venous return from the leg
The small saphenous vein drains into the femoral vein
explanation: About 90 % of venous return from the lower limb passes through the deep veins, aided by the calf muscle pump, so the superficial great saphenous vein can be removed without significant impairment. Perforating veins normally direct blood from superficial to deep, and the small saphenous vein drains into the popliteal vein.
